Consolidation durvalumab was associated with significant improvements in the primary end points of overall survival (OS; stratified hazard ratio [HR], 0.68; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.87; <i>P</i> = .00251) and progression-free survival (PFS [blinded independent central review; RECIST v1.1]; stratified HR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.42 to 0.65; <i>P</i> < .0001), with manageable safety. We report updated, exploratory analyses of survival, approximately 5 years after the last patient was randomly assigned.<h4>Methods</h4>Patients with WHO performance status 0 or 1 (any tumor programmed cell death-ligand 1 status) were randomly assigned (2:1) to durvalumab (10 mg/kg intravenously; administered once every 2 weeks for 12 months) or placebo, stratified by age, sex, and smoking history. Time-to-event end point analyses were performed using stratified log-rank tests. Medians and landmark survival rates were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method.<h4>Results</h4>Seven hundred and nine of 713 randomly assigned patients received durvalumab (473 of 476) or placebo (236 of 237). The phase III PACIFIC trial compared durvalumab with placebo in patients with unresectable, stage III non–small-cell lung cancer and no disease progression after concurrent chemoradiotherapy. # Five-Year Survival Outcomes From the PACIFIC Trial: Durvalumab After Chemoradiotherapy in Stage III Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer — Structured Research Report

**Source**: Spigel DR, Faivre-Finn C, Gray JE, et al. *J Clin Oncol.* 2022;40(12):1301-1311.
**DOI**: [10.1200/JCO.21.01308](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.21.01308)
**PMID**: [35108059](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35108059/)
**PMCID**: [PMC9015199](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9015199/)
**Open access via Europe PMC**: [https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC9015199](https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC9015199)
**License**: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
**Data cutoff**: January 11, 2021
**Clinical trial**: NCT02125461

---

## Abstract

**Background**: The phase III PACIFIC trial demonstrated that consolidation durvalumab, a programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor, significantly improved overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) compared with placebo in patients with unresectable, stage III non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without disease progression after concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT). This report presents updated exploratory survival analyses approximately five years after the last patient was randomly assigned.

**Methods**: Patients with WHO performance status 0 or 1, irrespective of tumor PD-L1 expression level, were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive durvalumab (10 mg/kg intravenously every two weeks for up to 12 months) or placebo, stratified by age, sex, and smoking history. Time-to-event outcomes were compared using stratified log-rank tests; medians and landmark survival rates were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method. Exploratory multivariable Cox regression analyses examined prognostic baseline factors.

**Results**: Among 713 randomly assigned patients, 709 received study treatment (durvalumab, n = 473; placebo, n = 236). As of the January 11, 2021 data cutoff, median follow-up was 34.2 months for all patients and 61.6 months for censored patients. Updated OS (stratified HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.59–0.89) and PFS (stratified HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.45–0.68) remained consistent with primary analyses. Median OS was 47.5 months for durvalumab versus 29.1 months for placebo; median PFS was 16.9 versus 5.6 months. Estimated five-year OS rates were 42.9% (95% CI, 38.2–47.4) versus 33.4% (95% CI, 27.3–39.6), and five-year PFS rates were 33.1% (95% CI, 28.0–38.2) versus 19.0% (95% CI, 13.6–25.2). In the primary safety analysis, grade 3/4 adverse events (AEs) occurred in 30.5% of durvalumab-treated patients versus 26.1% of placebo recipients; fatal AEs were reported in 4.4% versus 6.4%. Discontinuation due to AEs occurred in 15.4% versus 9.8% of patients.

**Conclusions**: Durvalumab after CRT provides robust and sustained OS and PFS benefit. An estimated 42.9% of patients in the durvalumab arm remained alive at five years, and 33.1% remained alive and progression-free, establishing a new benchmark for the standard of care in unresectable, stage III NSCLC.

---

## 1. Introduction

For patients with unresectable, stage III NSCLC, the historical standard of care consisted of platinum-based concurrent CRT followed by observation. This approach was associated with poor long-term survival, and neither induction nor consolidation chemotherapy, nor radiation dose escalation, had been shown to improve outcomes. The phase III PACIFIC trial represented a milestone: it was the first study to demonstrate a survival advantage with immunotherapy in a curative-intent setting for NSCLC.

The primary analyses (data cutoffs February 13, 2017 for PFS and March 22, 2018 for OS) established that durvalumab consolidation therapy, administered for up to 12 months, significantly improved OS (stratified HR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.53–0.87; P = 0.00251) and PFS (stratified HR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.42–0.65; P < 0.0001) compared with placebo. These findings, together with manageable safety and preserved patient-reported outcomes, led to global regulatory approvals and established the PACIFIC regimen as the standard of care.

To characterize long-term outcomes, we report updated exploratory analyses with approximately five years of follow-up since the last patient was randomly assigned, including updates of the primary endpoints, key secondary endpoints, and new exploratory analyses of prognostic baseline factors.

---

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Study Design

PACIFIC was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter phase III trial. Patients with histologically or cytologically documented unresectable stage III NSCLC (AJCC 7th edition) who had received at least two cycles of platinum-based concurrent CRT (typical total dose 60–66 Gy in 30–33 fractions) without disease progression were enrolled 1–42 days after CRT completion. Patients with unresolved Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE v4.03) grade >2 toxicities or grade ≥2 pneumonitis/radiation pneumonitis from prior CRT were excluded. Tumor tissue collection and PD-L1 testing were not required for enrollment, and no restriction was placed on the basis of oncogenic driver mutation status.

Eligible patients were randomly assigned (2:1) to receive durvalumab (10 mg/kg intravenously every two weeks for up to 12 months) or matching placebo. Randomization was stratified by age (<65 vs ≥65 years), sex, and smoking history (current/former vs never). Study treatment was discontinued in the event of confirmed disease progression, initiation of alternative anticancer therapy, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent. Patients were followed for survival after discontinuing study treatment.

### 2.2 Endpoints and Assessments

Primary endpoints were OS and PFS (assessed by blinded independent central review [BICR] per RECIST v1.1), analyzed in the intent-to-treat (ITT) population. Updated analyses included OS and PFS in exploratory subgroups defined by prespecified baseline factors (including PD-L1 tumor cell [TC] expression using the Ventana SP263 assay at a prespecified 25% threshold and a post hoc 1% threshold), time to death or distant metastasis (TTDM; BICR), objective response rate (ORR; BICR), duration of response (BICR), incidence of new lesions (BICR), time to first subsequent therapy or death (TFST), and time to second subsequent therapy or death (TSST). A post hoc analysis of time to second progression (investigator-assessed) was performed in patients who received durvalumab retreatment. New exploratory analyses examined the prognostic association of baseline factors (other than assigned study treatment) with OS and PFS using univariate and multivariable Cox regression models.

### 2.3 Statistical Analysis

Time-to-event comparisons between arms used log-rank tests stratified by the same factors as randomization. Medians and landmark survival rates (e.g., five-year OS) were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method. Subgroup analyses used unstratified Cox regression models without adjustment for multiple comparisons. Univariable and multivariable Cox regression models evaluated the prognostic association of baseline factors with OS and PFS; all prespecified variables were retained in final models without data-driven variable selection.

---

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Patient Disposition and Baseline Characteristics

Of 713 randomly assigned patients, 709 received study treatment (durvalumab, 473/476; placebo, 236/237). Baseline characteristics were well balanced between arms. As of the January 11, 2021 data cutoff, 419 patients (58.8%) had died (durvalumab: 264/476 [55.5%]; placebo: 155/237 [65.4%]). Median follow-up was 34.2 months (range 0.2–74.7) for all randomly assigned patients and 61.6 months (range 0.4–74.7) for censored patients. Treatment for 12 months was completed by 49.0% of patients in the durvalumab arm versus 34.7% in the placebo arm; discontinuation due to disease progression occurred in 31.3% versus 49.6%, and discontinuation due to AEs in 15.4% versus 9.7%.

### 3.2 Overall Survival and Progression-Free Survival

Updated OS was consistent with the primary analysis: the risk of death was reduced by 28% with durvalumab versus placebo (stratified HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.59–0.89). Median OS was 47.5 months with durvalumab versus 29.1 months with placebo. The estimated five-year OS rate was 42.9% (95% CI, 38.2–47.4) for durvalumab versus 33.4% (95% CI, 27.3–39.6) for placebo.

Updated PFS was also consistent with the primary analysis: a 45% reduction in the risk of progression or death was observed (stratified HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.45–0.68). Median PFS was 16.9 months versus 5.6 months. The estimated five-year PFS rate was 33.1% (95% CI, 28.0–38.2) versus 19.0% (95% CI, 13.6–25.2).

### 3.3 Subgroup Analyses

OS and PFS benefit favored durvalumab across all prespecified subgroups. With respect to PD-L1 expression subgroups, OS benefit was observed in patients with PD-L1 TC ≥25% and ≥1%, but OS results in patients with PD-L1 TC <1% showed an HR of 1.15 (95% CI, 0.75–1.75), though PFS still favored durvalumab in this subgroup (HR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.53–1.20). Key limitations in these PD-L1 analyses include use of pre-CRT archival tumor tissue, incomplete tissue availability (PD-L1 status unassessable for 37% of patients), small subgroup sizes (TC <1%: n = 148), and potential baseline prognostic factor imbalances in the placebo arm.

For the subgroup with EGFR mutations or ALK alterations (n = 43: 35 EGFR-mutated, 8 ALK-altered), the survival benefit with durvalumab is uncertain.
